here are some excessive notes. can you help me decide what sliders to add for getting the best possible VMT denominators?

---

Goal: bound ADS-engaged vehicle miles traveled (VMT) in the US, 2025-06-15 thru 2025-12-15, for a given operator, matching NHTSA SGO ADS incidents filtered to Driver/Operator Type = None.

Define:

* D = denominator miles you want = total US public-road miles with ADS engaged, in-scope, during the window.

Global/common parameters (apply to all operators)

* Geographic scope fraction:

   * f_US = fraction of the operator’s reported ADS miles that occurred in the US (if the reported metric is global).

* Road-scope fraction:

   * f_public = fraction of those US miles that occurred on “publicly accessible roads” (exclude closed-course, private lots, depots).

* ADS-engaged fraction:

   * f_ADS = fraction of the operator’s reported miles that are truly “ADS engaged” as defined by SGO (as opposed to manual driving, remote-only maneuvering, etc.), if the reported metric mixes modes.

* Operator=none mapping (only if your mileage source mixes operator types):

   * f_none = fraction of ADS-engaged miles where Driver/Operator Type would be “None” (no driver responsible) as opposed to in-vehicle safety driver / remote operator / test driver.
   * If you already have a mileage metric that is explicitly “driverless / rider-only / no driver,” set f_none = 1.

Service vs non-service decomposition parameters

* Deadhead/empty-mile share:

* d = non-service share of ADS-engaged VMT (0..1), where:

  * VMT_total = VMT_service + VMT_nonservice
  * d = VMT_nonservice / VMT_total
* Equivalently, multiplier from service miles to total VMT:

  * m_deadhead = 1 / (1 - d)
  * VMT_total = VMT_service * m_deadhead
* If you have total VMT directly, you don’t need d.

* If you only have passenger-miles (or “rider-only miles”) instead of vehicle-miles:

   * o = average vehicle occupancy during service (passenger count per vehicle-mile while in service), to convert:

     * passenger_miles = VMT_service * o
     * VMT_service = passenger_miles / o
   * If your service-mile metric is already vehicle-miles (not passenger-miles), set o = 1 and ignore.

Operator-specific “base-mile” parameter (choose one per operator)
8) Base mileage metric in-window before applying the fractions above (you need at least one of these):

* B_totalVMT: reported ADS vehicle-miles (service + non-service) in-window, OR
* B_serviceVMT: reported ADS vehicle-miles with customers (service miles) in-window, OR
* B_passengerMiles: reported passenger-miles in-window, OR
* B_cumulative(t): reported cumulative total at known dates t1 and t2 that bracket the window (so you can difference and/or interpolate).

Then compute bounds as:

* If B_totalVMT available:
  D = B_totalVMT * f_US * f_public * f_ADS * f_none
* If only B_serviceVMT available:
  D = B_serviceVMT * m_deadhead * f_US * f_public * f_ADS * f_none
* If only B_passengerMiles available:
  D = (B_passengerMiles / o) * m_deadhead * f_US * f_public * f_ADS * f_none

Minimum set needed to produce lower/upper bounds (typical)

* A base mileage metric B_* for the window (or bracketing cumulative values).
* d (deadhead share) unless B_totalVMT already includes non-service miles.
* f_none unless the base metric is explicitly driverless/no-driver.
* f_US if base metric isn’t US-only.
* f_public if base metric includes private/closed-course miles.
* f_ADS if base metric mixes ADS-engaged and non-ADS miles.
* o only if using passenger-miles instead of vehicle-miles.

  1. Add these sliders per operator:
  • B (base in-window miles): keep as main slider.

don't change any code but to be apples-to-apples, should it be fine to just leave all the non-service-share sliders at 0% for each company?
18:45 Codex gpt-5.3-codex (xhigh) thought for 20s

Yes, you can do that, with one caveat.

  • If you set all non-service share sliders to 0%, you’re comparing service/on-trip miles per incident consistently across companies.
  • That is apples-to-apples in that specific sense.

But:

  • Your numerator (NHTSA incidents) can include incidents during non-service miles too.
  • So 0% for all is not apples-to-apples for total ADS VMT; it will undercount denominators, and the bias is larger for companies with higher true deadhead.

So it’s fine if you interpret results as “per service mile.”
For “per total autonomous mile,” you should use nonzero deadhead assumptions.

does this model even make sense? can we rethink this from first principles?
19:15 Codex gpt-5.3-codex (xhigh) thought for 1m8s

Yes, we should rethink it from first principles.

  • Base model is coherent: if incidents are a Poisson process per mile, then with Jeffreys prior \(p(\lambda)\propto \lambda^{-1/2}\), posterior is \(\lambda \mid k,m \sim \text{Gamma}(k+0.5,\text{rate}=m)\).

This part in index.html:292–index.html:305 is conceptually fine, and the gammaquant numerics look accurate.

  • The phi part is the conceptual mismatch: index.html:294–index.html:295 scales both shape and rate by phi. That inflates variance, but because the UI uses 1 / median(lambda) as the point estimate (index.html:298, index.html:302), the center moves with phi.

So the current tooltip claim “higher values widen intervals” (index.html:408, etc.) is incomplete/wrong.

  • From first principles, overdispersion is not identifiable from one aggregate count per company. So the clean options are:
  1. Remove phi entirely (most principled with current data).
  2. Keep phi as a subjective “interval widen” control, but force center invariance (e.g., center at m/(k+0.5) and widen bounds around that center on log scale).

If you want, I can implement option 2 now and add a qual that fails if the point estimate changes when only phi changes.

19:18 Codex gpt-5.3-codex (xhigh) thought for 27s

Yes, killing phi is the clean move.

A global credible-interval-mass slider (default 95%) is a much better control than overdispersion here.

  • Keep model: lambda | k,m ~ Gamma(k+0.5, rate=m)
  • Keep point estimate fixed (eg 1 / median(lambda)), independent of interval mass
  • Let slider control only interval tails: tail = (1 - mass)/2
  • Interval for miles/incident: [1/q_{1-tail}(lambda), 1/q_{tail}(lambda)]

Recommendation:

  1. Remove all per-company vif/phi sliders.
  2. Add one global slider for interval mass (eg range 50% to 99.9%, default 95%).
  3. Update quals so changing mass widens/narrows bounds but does not move the point estimate.

If you want, I can implement this now.

  4. 30270-11424 (Changed 0.5 -> 1.0): Two Waymos in a parking lot. One was reversing out of a spot. The subject Waymo proceeded forward and hit the side of the reversing Waymo. Hitting the side of a reversing vehicle is the fault of the vehicle moving forward.

The remaining 10 cases marked as 0.5 are all genuine shared-fault scenarios where the AV made a questionable maneuver but the other vehicle also contributed. Examples include:

  • Stopping unexpectedly on a green light and getting rear-ended.
  • Stopping abruptly while straddling two lanes and getting rear-ended.
  • Merging into a tight gap in traffic and getting hit from behind.
  • Moving forward into the path of a reversing truck, but stopping before the truck hits it.
  • Proceeding forward while an adjacent vehicle's door is open, but the door swings into the AV.

The 1.0 cases are all solid (hitting stationary objects, turning from the wrong lane, driving into water/potholes, hardware failures). The 0.0 cases correctly exclude passenger actions (like opening doors into traffic).

Sanity check done against Kelsey Piper’s March 2026 article.

What matches vs doesn’t

| Metric | Kelsey framing | Crashla Waymo (Jun 15, 2025–Jan 15, 2026) | Crashla Waymo (Jun 15–Sep 30, 2025 only) | Verdict |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| “Any crash” | ~half human (inferred from Kusano/Scanlon: 2.1 vs 4.68 IPMM) | 4.77 IPMM (all incidents) | 5.51 IPMM (all incidents) | Discrepant if using all |
| Nonstationary crashes | (closest apples-to-apples to moving-crash framing) | 1.85 IPMM | 2.27 IPMM | Close to Kelsey’s “~half” framing |
| Injury | “~one-fifth as likely” | 0.524 IPMM | 0.641 IPMM | Broadly consistent (about 13–19% depending benchmark) |
| Airbag deployment | “~one-fifth as likely” | 0.204 IPMM | 0.241 IPMM | Broadly consistent (about 12–15%) |
| Serious injury (SSI+) | “~one-tenth as likely” | 0.029 IPMM | 0.027 IPMM | Broadly consistent (about 12%) |
| Fatal | Kelsey cites ~0.5 fatalities over 127M miles | 0.333 weighted fatalities over 103.1M effective miles = 0.00323 IPMM | 0.00891 IPMM | Same order, but method differs |

Why the discrepancies are real (not math bugs)

  1. Different window.

Kelsey’s Waymo figures are cumulative “through Sep 2025” (127M). Crashla is scoped to June 15, 2025 through January 15, 2026 and explicitly partial-month prorated. See [preprocess.py:172](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/preprocess.py:172), [preprocess.py:498](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/preprocess.py:498), [crashla.js:1265](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js:1265).

  1. Different numerator definition for “all”.

Crashla all uses all SGO incidents with operator None, including many stationary/0-mph events; Waymo has 301/492 at 0 mph in this window. Nonstationary is the closer analogue to Kelsey’s crash framing. See [crashla.js:1125](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js:1125).

  1. Different denominator definition.

Crashla uses modeled VMT (with coverage and incident-coverage adjustments), not Waymo’s published rider-only cumulative denominator.

  1. Fatality accounting is different by design.

Crashla uses per-vehicle fatality weighting (1 / vehiclesInvolved) and overrides the Sep 2025 Tempe fatality to 3 vehicles. See [preprocess.py:96](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/preprocess.py:96), [crashla.js:1236](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js:1236).

Net: the injury/airbag/serious-injury story is consistent with Kelsey’s order-of-magnitude claims. The apparent mismatch is mainly on all incidents, where Crashla’s all metric is broader and includes many stationary events; nonstationary aligns much better.

Sources:

  • https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/we-absolutely-do-know-that-waymos
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12675
  • https://waymo.com/safety/impact/

01:52 Codex gpt-5.3-codex (xhigh) thought for 59s

Yes, that fatality mismatch is real, but it’s mostly an apples-to-oranges comparison, not a math bug.

Piper’s 3.2x comes from this setup:

  • Waymo: 127M miles / 0.5 fatalities ≈ 254M miles per fatality
  • Humans: ~80M miles per fatality
  • Multiplier: 254/80 ≈ 3.2x

Your Jun-Sep table used a different setup:

  • Denominator: 37.4M (only Jun 15–Sep 30 in this model, with June prorated)
  • Fatal numerator: 0.333 (per-vehicle weighting of the Sep fatal incident)
  • Plus Bayesian shrinkage for tiny k (posterior median), which pulls MPI down further

That’s why you see roughly 0.54x–0.94x in that specific table.

If you do Jun-Sep with Piper-style arithmetic (no prior, direct m/k), you get:

  • 37.4M / 0.333 ≈ 112M, so 112/80 ≈ 1.4x (not 0.94x)

And with the latest full window (Jun 15–Jan 15), Piper-style is even higher:

  • 103.1M / 0.333 ≈ 309M, so 309/80 ≈ 3.9x

So:

  1. Nonfatal metrics: no big contradiction; directionally consistent.
  2. Fatality: very sensitive to method/window; your displayed Jun-Sep number is not directly comparable to Piper’s 3.2x.

I initially categorized it as 0.0 fault because it sounded like an unpredictable/adversarial action by a pedestrian intentionally blocking the road.

However, after looking closer at the actual narrative logic, you make a great point:

"The Waymo AV was traveling northbound in the left lane on Main Street when it approached a wire apparently tied on one end to a utility pole and being held up by a pedestrian on the west sidewalk of Main Street, such that the wire was suspended low across all lanes... The Waymo proceeded straight, striking the suspended wire and then driving over it."

The wire was already stretched across all lanes when the AV approached it. This means the AV failed to detect a stationary physical obstacle in its path and drove straight into it (and over it). While the pedestrian created the hazard, fundamentally the AV's perception system failed a very basic driving task (don't drive into visible things obstructing the road). To answer your actual question about the biggest discrepancy between our app and Kelsey Piper's article:

Piper is evaluating Waymo's *all-time* safety record, whereas our app is strictly windowed to June 2025 – January 2026 (to ensure apples-to-apples baseline comparisons across the active window).

Because of this difference in time scope, the biggest discrepancies are:

  1. Fatalities: Piper notes Waymo has been present for *two* fatal incidents (a 3-car crash counting as 0.33 deaths, and a 7-car crash counting as 0.14 deaths, totaling 0.47). Because our dashboard only starts tracking from June 2025 forward, the 7-car crash isn't in our dataset. We only record the September 3-car motorcycle crash in Tempe, meaning our app assesses Waymo with 0.33 fatalities instead of 0.47.
  2. VMT Math: Piper notes that Waymo hit 127 million miles *all-time* as of September 2025. Because we only tally miles within the June–Jan window, our system uses an effective VMT of roughly ~106 million miles for Waymo's rates. (Coincidentally, our dataset projects Waymo's *in-window* cumulative mileage hitting ~127 million miles right at the end of January, but these represent two completely different mileages).

Otherwise, the rates and core arguments closely match. Our SGO dataset confirms Waymo has 1 serious injury per ~35 million miles (roughly the "one-tenth" of the human benchmark, as she cites) and 1 airbag deployment per ~5 million miles (far lower than the human rate, also matching her argument).

I've gone through the article and compared it to our data in and . Here is how the numbers stack up:

Where we agree:

  • Total Incident Count: Both the article and our dataset have exactly 14 incidents involving Tesla robotaxis since June 2025.
  • Incident Details: The table of all 14 collisions in the article perfectly matches our parsed NHTSA records row-by-row on Date, Object Hit (Crash With), Speeds, Severity, and Pre-Crash Movement (e.g., the January 2026 bus collision at 0 MPH, the October 2025 "Other" crash at 18 MPH proceeding straight, and the July 2025 SUV collision with hospitalization at 2 MPH making a right turn).

Where we disagree:

  • Total Miles Driven (VMT): The article estimates 800,000 total robotaxi miles for Tesla. Our cumulative metric (using Austin robotaxitracker data) projects a lower figure of 672,500 miles through the end of January 2026.
  • Crash Rate Implications: Because the article uses a higher mileage denominator (800,000 / 14), they get a collision rate of roughly 1 in every 57,000 miles. Our data points toward a slightly higher frequency of roughly 1 in every 48,035 miles (672,500 / 14).
  • The "First vs Last 7" Split: The author notes Tesla hit its first 7 collisions over about 250,000 miles and the next 7 over 550,000 miles. According to our timeline, Tesla crossed the 250k-mile threshold around the end of October 2025 (256,984 cumulative miles). By that point, our dataset already shows 8 collisions (3 in July, 4 in Sept, 1 in Oct) rather than 7.

From a skeptical scientist perspective, next step is to try to break your conclusions.

  1. Build a “conclusion fragility” analysis.
  • Vary every controversial assumption jointly (vmt_min/max, incident coverage, fault weighting, human baseline choice).
  • Output: probability each headline claim remains true across the full assumption space.
  • This tells you whether you have robust findings or assumption-dependent stories.
  1. Add explicit competing models, not just Poisson.
  • Compare Poisson vs overdispersed alternatives (e.g., negative binomial) and a time-varying rate model.
  • Output: model comparison + whether company rankings change.
  1. Validate fault fractions against blinded human coding.
  • Random sample incidents, have humans score AV fault independently, compare to LLM ensemble.
  • Output: calibration bias and uncertainty inflation factor for fault-weighted metrics.
  1. Tighten apples-to-apples human benchmarking.
  • Match by ODD-like strata (speed, roadway type, severity threshold), not one broad human band.
  • Output: matched human MPI bands per stratum and pooled estimate.
  1. Add a preregistered robustness appendix.
  • Write “replicata / expectata / resultata” style hypotheses before reruns.
  • Lock a data snapshot and regenerate all numbers from scripts only.

If you want one concrete implementation next, do #1 first; it gives the strongest defense against skepticism with the least ambiguity.

My recommendation:

  • I would keep slurp.py responsible for producing structured report data, but use a separate renderer for the HTML/PDF layer.

Concretely, the clean shape is:

  • slurp.py writes the normal data files plus a report artifact like static/report.json or similar.
  • A renderer builds static/index.html from that artifact, including:
  • exact inclusion/filtering rules
  • dedup rules
  • VMT assumptions and monthly rationale
  • incident-coverage adjustment
  • Bayesian MPI method
  • fault-fraction method
  • human baseline method
  • source timestamps / snapshot provenance
  • the actual computed tables/charts
  • Later, static/report.pdf is produced from static/index.html via one print/render step.

That keeps one source of truth for the numbers and one source of truth for the prose/report structure.

If you want, the next step I’d take is phase 1 only: generate a self-contained static HTML report in /static, and explicitly defer PDF until the HTML shape is right.

Findings

At-fault metrics are currently biased low because missing fault rows inside the active comparison window are silently accepted and then aggregated as zero. data/slurp.py only targets report IDs already present in the faultfrac-*.csv files ([data/slurp.py#L291](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/data/slurp.py#L291), [data/slurp.py#L316](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/data/slurp.py#L316)), its missing_fault check is tautological ([data/slurp.py#L797](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/data/slurp.py#L797), [data/slurp.py#L801](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/data/slurp.py#L801)), and monthSeriesData() then does rec.atFault += atFaultFrac || 0 ([crashla.js#L806](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L806), [crashla.js#L816](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L816)). I verified 91 currently visible-window incidents have fault: null: 89 Waymo and 2 Zoox, all in 2026-01/2026-02. That means default atfault / atfaultInjury MPI is understated.
  1. Incident-browser date sorting is wrong. The date sort key is the raw MMM-YYYY string ([crashla.js#L1772](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L1772)), and renderTable() string-sorts non-numeric columns with localeCompare ([crashla.js#L1975](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L1975), [crashla.js#L1982](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L1982)).   1. 11:33 Copilot Chat copilot/gemini-3.1-pro-preview thought for 1m3s

Here is a step-by-step breakdown of exactly what that command does:

  1. head -n 831 data/faultfrac-gemini.csv

This reads exactly the first 831 lines of the file and outputs them. (Anything from line 832 onward is ignored).

  1. > temp.csv

This redirects that output (the 831 lines) and saves it into a new temporary file named temp.csv.

  1. &&

This operator tells the terminal to only run the next part of the command *if* the first part succeeded without any errors.

  1. mv temp.csv data/faultfrac-gemini.csv

This moves (renames) temp.csv to overwrite .

The final result:
It permanently truncates so that it contains *only* its first 831 lines. Any data that existed on line 832 or below is completely deleted.

*(Note: In my previous cancelled command, I used head -n -20, where the minus sign means "keep everything *except* the last 20 lines". I was trying to surgically remove the last 20 corrupted lines I had accidentally appended, not keep only 20 lines! But using a text editor or being more careful is definitely safer.)*

  • Injury: Waymo human 3.90 IPMM = about 256k MPI, inside our 252k..524k band in [crashla.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L255).

Los Angeles 1.23 -> 813k above,
San Francisco 2.11 -> 474k below,
Austin 2.37 -> 422k below.

So the careful answer is:

  • All Locations only: almost no, except the hospitalization surrogate upper endpoint is a bit stale.
  • Anything on the Waymo page, including city rows: yes, definitely. Our human bands are too global to contain all of Waymo’s city-specific human benchmarks.

Verdict: the ~1M figure is contradicted by Tesla's own disclosures — off by roughly 3x as of today. If anything, the repo's Tesla series (2.69M cumulative through June 2026) is somewhat low, not high. Details below.

The anchor chain

Tesla's own quarterly disclosures of cumulative paid Robotaxi miles (a strict subset of the repo's total-scope driverless VMT, which adds deadhead/unpaid miles):

| Date | Tesla-disclosed paid cume | Repo total-scope cume |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-10-22 (Q3 call) | ~250k "total miles" | ~250k (anchor) |
| 2025-12-31 (Q4 deck) | 610k | 650k (robotaxitracker anchor) |
| ~2026-02-15 (Q4-call-era reporting) | ~700k | ~800k interpolated |
| 2026-03-31 (Q1 deck) | 1.7M | 1,563,047 |

The decisive datapoint: Tesla's Q1-2026 shareholder update says paid Robotaxi miles reached 1.7M by end of Q1, up from 610k at end of Q4 2025 (Drive Tesla, quoting the deck directly). Scope is the Texas driverless network — the deck frames it as unsupervised Austin plus the April Dallas/Houston launch, and the repo's README already documents (from the Q3-2025 call transcript) that Bay Area safety-driver miles are excluded from Tesla's Robotaxi metric. So it's apples-to-apples with the repo's scope, and it's a *floor* (paid miles exclude deadhead). Cumulative in-scope VMT was ≥1.7M nearly four months ago; April–June added Dallas/Houston plus continued Austin service. ~1M cumulative today can't be reconciled with Tesla's own numbers.

Where ~1M likely came from

The most plausible reconstruction: spotted-active-fleet × the trackers' "115 mi/vehicle/day" heuristic. Roughly 25–35 average active vehicles × 115 mi/day × ~13 months lands right at 1.1–1.6M. Your own project notes (memory, 2026-07-15) explicitly warn against exactly this: only the fleet×utilization *product* is anchored, spotted counts are a floor, and this method undershoots the hard-anchored Oct→Dec 2025 window by ~2x. The H1-2026 active-fleet trough (Electrek: fleet "shrinking" in May, Austin stalled at 17 active cars as of today) makes the per-vehicle arithmetic look even more pessimistic. Alternative origins — extrapolating from the stale 610–650k end-2025 anchor, or the ~700k paid figure from February — land in the same place.

Two genuine repo issues this turned up

  1. The Q1-2026 rows are below the paid-only floor. The Q1 rationale reads Tesla's "paid robotaxi miles ~doubled sequentially" as "Q1 ≈ 2x Q4," giving a Q1 delta of 913k. The deck's actual cumulative figures (610k → 1.7M) imply a Q1 delta of ~1.09M — "doubled sequentially" was evidently month-over-month, not quarter-over-quarter. Result: the repo's end-Q1 central (1.563M) sits *under* the 1.7M paid floor (the band top, 1.766M, barely contains it), and everything downstream through June inherits the shortfall. Since Q2 monthly rows were scaled off that base, the true current cumulative is plausibly ~3.2–3.6M. Direction of bias: understating the denominator makes Tesla's MPI look *worse* than reality — the conservative direction, but worth fixing. The Q2 earnings tomorrow (2026-07-22, already flagged in the repo as the recalibration anchor) should publish an end-Q2 cumulative to recalibrate against.
  1. The rides-lane calibration mis-dates the 700k figure. The 2026-07-01 rides calibration cites "robotaxitracker-via-Electrek (2026-04-30): ~700k paid miles by late Apr 2026." The actual 2026-04-30 Electrek article contains no mileage figure at all (I checked — it's fleet counts only); the ~700k traces to mid-February reporting off the Q4 call. With paid miles actually at 1.7M by end of March, the Tesla ride-count lane (156k at 2026-03) is likely ~2x low as well.

I haven't changed anything — this was an investigation. The clean next step is tomorrow's Q2 deck: recalibrate Q1–Q2 rows against the two cumulative paid pins (1.7M end-Q1, plus whatever end-Q2 prints), with total-scope = paid + a deadhead allowance.

Yes — and it's deliberate, not an accident. Here's the picture:

The row. [vmt.csv](data/vmt.csv) Tesla 2026-07: best 170k, band [55k, 340k] = 0.32×–2.0×. Every deck-anchored month before it is 0.85×–1.25× (Feb 324k … Jun 157k). So July is ~4× wider than its neighbors.

Why. July is the first "extension month" past Tesla's last hard anchor. The only real Tesla VMT source is the "Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles" chart in the quarterly deck; the Q2 deck pinned 2.440M cumulative at end-June, and the next anchor is the Q3 deck (~late Oct). In between, the number is extrapolation, and the extrapolation method has a bad recent track record: the pre-pin activity-ratio estimates for Q2 ran ~28% high (June rationale), and the earlier fleet-count ratios ran ~2× hot — a utilization-led slowdown the fleet counts didn't see. So the July row is explicitly a placeholder: best held near the May–Jun run-rate (170k), floor = taking robotaxitracker's late-July "approaching 2.5M" literally (2.5M − 2.44M ≈ 55k for the month), ceiling = ~2× June's pace on the new-metro upside (Miami driverless Jul 3, Tampa/Orlando Jul 21). The Aug 10 source survey found nothing to tighten it.

Whether it's *too* wide. Arguments it's about right:

  • The floor is a real datapoint in the same scope, not a hedge — if the tracker's cumulative is right, July really was ~60k and 170k is a 3× overestimate.
  • The ceiling is the mirror: six metros vs. three, if the fleet actually ramps.
  • It's monthly, and July is also at 11% incident coverage, so the July point on the chart is dominated by *both* uncertainties anyway.
  • Effect on the cumulative-based Tesla numbers is modest: kyoom band goes from [2.37M, 2.81M] at end-June (−3%/+15%) to [2.42M, 3.15M] (−7%/+21%) — July adds roughly ±140k on a 2.6M base.

Argument it's too generous on the *upside*: 340k would be Tesla's second-best month ever (only Mar 438k beats it) at a time when the unsupervised fleet has stalled at ~17–21 cars and utilization was already falling; 1.5× June (~235k) is arguably a fairer ceiling. The downside floor I'd leave alone.

When it resolves. Same as May/June did: the Q3 deck (~late Oct) pins Jul–Sep and the band snaps back to 0.85×–1.25×. Until then it's honest about how little is known.

2. My claim that "the floor is a real datapoint" was wrong. The row's rationale says the 55k floor "takes trackers' late-Jul 'approaching 2.5M' literally". That phrase is Tesla's own end-of-Q2 figure — the deck/call on Jul 22 said "nearly 2.5 million cumulative paid miles by the end of the second quarter" — restated by press, not a late-July reading. The Aug 10 survey already established no post-deck mileage estimate exists anywhere and that robotaxitracker no longer publishes a mileage model. So "2.5M − 2.44M ≈ 55k for July" is an artifact of subtracting the vector-extracted chart value from its own rounded restatement. It carries zero information about July.

What's impeccable given that:

  • The *numbers* [55k, 340k] remain defensible, but on different grounds than stated: floor ≈ 170k ÷ 2.9 = the largest single-month overprediction in the Q2 scorecard (May); ceiling ≈ 2× June = a launch-ramp month (three metros went unsupervised in July; the file's only ≥2× month-over-month jumps are launch months) plus Tesla's ">10%/wk" claim. Both are honest "we have one quarter of miss data and this is what a miss of that size looks like" placeholders. Changing them would be swapping one judgment for another with no new information.
  • The *rationale text* is factually mis-sourced and should say the above instead — that the floor is scorecard-calibrated, not a datapoint; that "nearly 2.5M" is the end-Q2 figure; and that no independent July estimate exists (Aug 10 survey). That's a one-cell edit in [vmt.csv](data/vmt.csv) (Tesla 2026-07 rationale) plus a vmt.js regen; no number changes; no qual impact.

That's what I'd do, and only that. Say go and it's done; otherwise the numbers as they stand are the honest state of ignorance until the Q3 deck (~late Oct).

Its nowcast value was client-rendered from an API Wayback never captured. So a late-July reading is unrecoverable, and it would have been a Dec-2025-anchored fleet extrapolation anyway. Its implied current run-rate is 143 × 115 ≈ 490k/mo vs Tesla's actual June 157k. Roughly 3× hot. Upper bound only.
  • shadowmode.us retired its modeled mileage panel on Aug 12. Changelog: denominators were "assumed constants (fleet × 100 mi/day × 180 days)".
  • TxDMV MCCS registry (official, SB 2807; JSON API; front-ends texasavtracker.com and robotaxitracker): Tesla Robotaxi LLC 186 registered VINs (42 May 28 → 69 Jun 11 → 102 Jul 2 → 175 Jul 15 → 181 Jul 30 → 186 Aug 11); Waymo 691; Zoox 44; Avride 344. The dominant cause isn't Waymo's CI (k=1,078 makes it tight) — it's that (a) the human band itself spans 2.1× (Kusano/Scanlon per-city range), and (b) all-incidents is the metric where reporting-threshold disparity bites hardest: 58% of Waymo's incidents are 0-mph and 89% property-only, events human police-report data never captures. That's exactly why every apples-er metric (nonstationary, at-fault, injury, airbag) reads robustly safer for Waymo. 2. The 0.1x fatality cards. The card multiplier is posterior-median MPI ÷ the geometric mean of the human band (√(87M×130M) ≈ 106M). With zero fatalities and only ~2.4M (Tesla) / ~3.4M (Zoox) effective miles, the Jeffreys posterior median lands at ~4.4× exposure — 10.8M/11.5M MPI — because zero deaths in a few million miles carries almost no information about a ~1-per-100M-mile event. 10.8M/106M ≈ 0.1x. It is *not* evidence they're 10× deadlier than humans; it's the model saying "not enough miles to know," and the CI printed directly beneath (826k – 6.9B) says exactly that. Waymo shows 3.4x because 195M effective miles with 0.3 fractional deaths genuinely beats the human rate. If the 0.1x-at-k=0 look bothers you, suppressing the multiplier when k=0 would be a one-line change — your call, since it's a display-semantics choice.

3. Dispersion 12.82 (now 12.34): a small monkey wrench, precisely locatable. Decomposition: 87% of the entire X² comes from one month — July 2025, the launch month, 3 incidents on 6,317 miles (expected 0.06). Excluding that single month, the index is 1.91; Feb–Jul 2026 alone is 2.08 — near the "consistent with Poisson" line. So the violation isn't clumping; it's that Tesla's rate fell ~50× from a terrible tiny-VMT launch month. It's mandatory, not fastidiousness. The Third Amended SGO 2021-01 (in force since June 16, 2025, so it governs a JAN-2026 incident) defines a crash as "any physical impact between a vehicle and another road user … or property that results or allegedly results in any property damage." No speed or severity floor. The 2025 amendment added a $1,000 damage floor for monthly ADS reports — then waived it in the next clause: reportable anyway if "the subject vehicle was the only vehicle involved in the crash" or "struck another vehicle or object." In practice it's moot. "Any property damage" has no floor, so the exemption requires proving a negative about someone who has left the scene, within five days. NHTSA says file on notice of a crash that *may* be reportable, before verifying; Instruction ¶2 says file incomplete and update later; ¶9 won't pause the clock while you ask. Each day of non-filing is a separate violation, up to $27,874/day. Every enforcement action in the program's history — Pony.ai, Cruise's $1.5M consent order, the still-open Tesla audit — is for under- or late-reporting. None for over-reporting.

Decisively: zero of Tesla's 24 ADS reports is coded Highway or Freeway. So the driver's-seat era contributed no incidents to our numerator at all — the specific thing you worried about doesn't touch the data, independent of the Level-2 legal argument.

Remote operators are separately capped at ≤2 mph direct control.

Net: the scope stays as implemented, the ~85% supervised-mile contamination remains the real and unfixable limitation, and the load on that one sentence just got heavier.

The pixelation

Replicata. Load at devicePixelRatio 2, zoom in on the top-left corner of the abstract or any heading rule.
Expectata. A drawn line, antialiased like the text beside it.
Resultata. The stroke is chopped into hard-edged segments sitting at whole-pixel offsets, with *no partial coverage on the steps*, and notches bitten out of the vertical edge.

Cause: feDisplacementMap. It resamples the source nearest-neighbour and offsets by whole *device* pixels. On a 2.5px stroke each wobble is a jog of ~40% of the stroke width landing with zero antialiasing. Not a browser bug — Chromium, Firefox and WebKit (all three launched from the playwright cache) produce it identically.

Three plausible explanations were tested and ruled out, rather than assumed:

  1. Not 1×-rasterize-then-upscale. Edge-run lengths aren't quantized to DPR (23% at 3×, 60% at 2× — about chance) and half the edge-band pixels are midtones. The filter does run at device resolution.
  2. Not gamma. SVG filters default to linearRGB, a classic crunchy-edge culprit. Adding color-interpolation-filters="sRGB" gave a pixel-identical result.
  3. Not filter-region size. The abstract (253px tall) and the market list (946px) were equally chewed.

Tuning helps but can't cure it: one octave, baseFrequency .04 → .012, and a blurred displacement field make the steps longer and fewer, never softer, because the offset stays an integer.

Fix. All three <filter> defs deleted; every filter: url() gone. index.html is now back to net-zero diff. The heading and footer rules are a 198px hand-drawn wave in a data-URI SVG used as a mask-image over background: var(--line) — shape in the token, color in the palette, path antialiased properly, and it starts and ends at y=4.3 with matching slope so repeat-x has no seam. The abstract and market list dropped their border-drawing ::before and carry a plain 2.5px border; the wobble was always coming from border-radius, which never aliased. Verified smooth at 9× in all three engines — that comparison is the figure in the artifact.

Links

--accent back to #2060c0.

That change surfaced a defect the first pass introduced: warming --wash to #f6f2ea had quietly dropped --iffy to 4.31:1 on it, and .pm-subcard paints .pm-card-odds.mid there. Nudged to #806716. It was caught by a new qual that computes WCAG contrast for every meaning-bearing token against --paper/--card/--wash, not by eye. (--ink-faint is deliberately excluded — it's the de-emphasized meta text and has always been sub-AA, before this work too.)

Qual spec change — flagging per rule 5

sketch-style.qual.mjs §4 previously asserted the displacement filters exist. It now asserts the opposite: no feDisplacementMap in index.html, no filter: url() in style.css, and that --drawn-rule is an SVG path used through mask-image with the -webkit- prefix over a tokenized background. §5 (no filter on a layout ancestor) is kept as a hazard guard. The quals were one turn old and mine rather than yours, but the technique they encoded turned out to be the bug, so the reversal is worth naming.
